---
applyTo: "spec/**/*.rb"
---

# Other services

- In request, feature, job and service specs, stub each request or message the code sends to another service at its transport, and check that it was sent. In those specs, you MUST NOT stub the service class that sends it, e.g. `allow(NewsletterClient).to receive(:new)` or `allow(PostNotifier).to receive(:default)`. Action specs stub the service instead.
- Stub HTTP with WebMock. When a service's SDK has its own stubs, use them instead, e.g. `stub_responses` in the AWS SDK. When neither can reach the client, e.g. a socket client such as the `mqtt` gem, use a fake client in `spec/support`, e.g. `FakeMqttClient`.
- Put the stubs for each service in a helper module in `spec/support`, included in every spec, with one method for each response the specs need: success, failure and, when the service can be slow, timeout, e.g. `stub_newsletter_create`, `stub_newsletter_create_failure` and `stub_newsletter_create_timeout` in `NewsletterServiceHelpers` in `spec/support/newsletter_service.rb`. Start each name with `stub_`, then the service and the request or message.
- You MUST NOT stub the transport in a spec, e.g. with `stub_request`, `Aws.config` or `allow` on a fake. When the helper you need doesn't exist yet, add it to the service's support file first.
- Return what the spec checks from every helper, e.g. the WebMock stub or the fake client. Call helpers inside the example. Avoid calling them in a `let` or `before` block. Keep what a helper returns in a local variable, e.g. `newsletter_request = stub_newsletter_create` or `mqtt_client = stub_mqtt_connection`.
- Give each failure helper an argument for the failure, with the real service's most likely failure as its default, e.g. `def stub_newsletter_create_failure(status: 500)`, called as `stub_newsletter_create_failure(status: 422)`.
- Build each body or message a helper returns or a spec queues in Ruby, e.g. as a hash, and convert it to the service's format, e.g. `body: { id: }.to_json`, or with `to_xml` or `URI.encode_www_form`. You SHOULD NOT write a body or message as a raw string, e.g. `"{\"id\":\"newsletter-1\"}"`. When you convert a string to Ruby, check that both give the same body, e.g. `"3.1"` stays a string.
- When a spec checks what was sent, add a `have_` matcher to the service's helper module, named after the verb and the same service and request as the stub, e.g. `have_requested_newsletter_create` or `have_published_mqtt_message`, with keywords for the parts to check, e.g. `body:` or `payload:`. Make a failing matcher list what was sent.
- Outside the service's own spec, check only the parts of the request or message the spec is about, with `hash_including`, e.g. `expect(WebMock).to have_requested_newsletter_create(body: hash_including(title: "Hello World"))`.
- Match a value the app generates by its format in request, job and feature specs, e.g. `"message_id" => a_string_matching(/\A\h{8}-\h{4}-\h{4}-\h{4}-\h{12}\z/)` for a UUID. Check that two fields hold the same value only in the service's own spec, where the spec passes the value in.
- Turn an SDK's stubs on for every spec in a `spec/support` file named after the SDK, and remove each service's stubbed responses after each spec, e.g. `Aws.config.update(stub_responses: true)` and `config.after { Aws.config.delete(:s3) }` in `spec/support/aws.rb`.
- Set AWS responses in `Aws.config` inside a helper, e.g. `stub_post_backup_upload`, and return a request's params from a block that keeps them, e.g. `Aws.config[:s3] = { stub_responses: { put_object: ->(context) { uploads << context.params; {} } } }` then `uploads` on the helper's last line. Stub a failure with the error's code, e.g. `put_object: "ServiceUnavailable"` in `stub_post_backup_upload_failure`.
- Use a fake client only when neither WebMock nor the SDK's own stubs can reach the client. In request, feature, job and service specs, you MUST NOT stub the gem's client class, e.g. `instance_double(MQTT::Client)`.
- Block the gem's real connections for every spec in a `before` hook in its support file, with a message that names the helpers to use, e.g. `config.before { allow(MQTT::Client).to receive(:connect).and_raise("Use stub_mqtt_connection or stub_mqtt_message") }` in `spec/support/mqtt.rb`, because `WebMock.disable_net_connect!` doesn't cover sockets.
- Define one fake in the gem's support file, named `Fake` then the client's class, e.g. `FakeMqttClient` in `spec/support/mqtt.rb`. Give it only the methods the app calls, with the real client's parameter names, even for parameters it ignores. Record each outbound call, e.g. each published message and subscribed topic.
- Give a fake's blocking read a defined end, so a spec never waits on a socket. With a block, yield every queued message in order, then return. Without a block, return the next message. Raise only when nothing was queued, e.g. `raise "No MQTT message queued. Add one with stub_mqtt_message" if queued_messages.empty?` at the top of `FakeMqttClient#get`.
- Give the fake its own spec outside `spec/support`, with one example for each method in `described_class.public_instance_methods(false)`, other than the readers for its recorded calls and queue, which checks that the real client has the same parameters, e.g. `expect(described_class.instance_method(name).parameters).to eq(MQTT::Client.instance_method(name).parameters)` in `spec/fakes/fake_mqtt_client_spec.rb`. Also check the fake's own behaviour: queued messages come back in order, subscribed topics are recorded, and reading with nothing queued raises.
- Return the fake from the gem's connect method, not from the service, so the service's own code runs, e.g. its pool, e.g. `allow(MQTT::Client).to receive(:connect).and_return(fake_mqtt_client)` in `stub_mqtt_connection`. Name each fake helper after the method it stubs, e.g. `stub_mqtt_connection_failure` for `MQTT::Client.connect` and `stub_mqtt_reconnect_failure` for `FakeMqttClient#connect`.
- End every fake helper by returning the fake, e.g. `fake_mqtt_client` on its last line, not the stub that `allow` returns.
- In a fake's failure helper, take an `error` argument and default it to the error the real method raises, read from the gem's source, e.g. `def stub_mqtt_publish_failure(error = MQTT::Exception.new("Not connected"))`. When the default isn't the gem's own error, e.g. a socket error, say why in a comment above the helper.
- Queue one more message on each call to a fake's message helper. Queue the messages for each run just before it, because a run drains the queue, e.g. call `stub_mqtt_message` again before a second `perform_now`.
- In a fake's matcher, take keywords with RSpec's matcher DSL, e.g. `matcher :have_published_mqtt_message do |topic, **options|`, and parse the payload from its format, e.g. JSON, unless the spec passes a string. Check the exact string in the service's own spec, e.g. `payload: { title: "Hello World", id: post.id }.to_json`, and parts elsewhere with `a_hash_including`. Write a `failure_message` that lists every message the fake recorded.
- Give each spec a new fake, and clear the service's cached connections after each spec, so no spec gets the last spec's client, e.g. `config.after { PostNotifier.const_get(:POOLS).clear }`.
- Test reconnecting and error handling with the fake and its failure helpers, e.g. `stub_mqtt_reconnect_failure(Errno::ECONNREFUSED)`. Test what depends on timing or the wire, e.g. keepalive timeouts and TLS, in one spec for the service's connection code against a real server or the gem's in-process server, e.g. `MQTT::FakeServer`. You MUST NOT test what the app does over a real socket.
